summary:
Catamarca is a province of Argentina and stands under the national framework. Argentina's Law 26.743, passed by the Chamber of Deputies 167-17-7 and by the Senate on 9 May 2012 by 55 votes to one abstention, was promulgated on 24 May 2012 and permits a change of legal gender without surgery, without hormone treatment and without judicial approval. The United Nations described it at the time as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region. No separate provincial record for Catamarca was located, so the national picture is the baseline a visitor should carry.

That statutory position has been narrowed by executive action rather than by repeal. In February 2025 the government of President Javier Milei issued a decree banning gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy for minors and a second decree governing the housing of transgender people in prison. Legal experts called the first decree illegal and unconstitutional and petitioned the courts to intervene; the outcome of that litigation is not recorded in the sources available here.

The institutional machinery of protection has been dismantled. The federal anti-discrimination institute INADI has been closed, the Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry eliminated, and trans people hired under the public-sector labour-inclusion quota dismissed in 2024. Trans activists in the national capital interviewed on 4 April 2025 said the government's policies had made the community more vulnerable and described the situation as chaotic and desperate; violence, discrimination and poverty affecting trans people are reported as worsened.

Violence reached a documented high in 2025. The National LGBT+ Hate Crimes Observatory recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity during the year, an increase of 62% over the previous year and the highest count in the observatory's ten years of operation, averaging one crime every 38 hours. Trans women and travestis accounted for 62.5% of victims (142 cases) and gay men 22% (50). The report ties the surge to institutional weakening and to state legitimation of discriminatory discourse. Agencia Presentes published the figures on 19 March 2026.

On 5 April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán, rejecting attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance that an appeal court had removed in 2020. The gender-motivated-crime aggravator therefore does not apply in that case as it now stands.

Argentina legalised marriage equality in 2010, the first Latin American country to do so, and anti-discrimination protections exist through national and provincial law. An Outright International country overview updated on 12 March 2026 nonetheless records negative assessments on same-sex relations, on gender recognition and on organisation registration, indicating deterioration.
tangentialFactors:
The tightening in Argentina since 2024 has come through executive decrees and the closure of agencies rather than through amendment of Law 26.743 itself, which remains in force and continues to govern legal gender recognition in Catamarca.

The 2025 hate-crime figures represent a 62% rise over 2024 and the highest annual count since the observatory began operating a decade earlier. The national pattern of violence is concentrated on trans women and travestis, who made up nearly two-thirds of victims.

Argentina was the first country in the region to legalise marriage equality, in 2010, and the shift recorded by international monitors since 2024 concerns the machinery of protection and the tone of state policy rather than the withdrawal of those formal rights.
localsOnly:
Residents of Catamarca are covered by provincial anti-discrimination provisions as well as by national law, and the province carries no separate documented pattern of trans-specific violence in the sources reviewed.

The public-sector labour-inclusion quota that had placed trans people in state employment was applied nationally, and the dismissals carried out in 2024 affected residents as well as visitors in employment terms.

The closure of INADI removed the federal complaints channel available to residents; no provincial substitute for that channel is recorded in the sources.
outOfScopeNotes:
The outcome of the litigation against the February 2025 decree on gender-affirming care for minors is not recorded in the sources available here and remains unresolved.

No separate reporting specific to Catamarca on trans-specific violence, policing or facility access was located; the assessment therefore rests on the national record and cannot confirm conditions particular to the province.

Whether the travesticidio aggravating circumstance will be pursued in other pending cases after the 5 April 2025 ruling is not sourced.

The specific instruments behind the Outright International negative assessments of 12 March 2026 are not itemised in the material reviewed.
